```{r}
#| include: false
source("assets/setup.R")
source("assets/quiz.R")
t_fbs  <- t.test(p$fbs_presentation, mu = 100)
t_sexf <- t.test(fbs_presentation ~ sex_of_participants, data = p)
dmp    <- filter(p, past_history_of_diabetes == "yes")
t_dmf  <- t.test(fbs_presentation ~ sex_of_participants, data = dmp)
pt_un  <- t.test(p$fbs_presentation, p$fbs_6_months)
w_age  <- t.test(age_of_participants ~ past_history_of_diabetes, data = p)
d_age  <- cohens_d(age_of_participants ~ past_history_of_diabetes, data = p, pooled_sd = FALSE)
pt     <- t.test(p$fbs_presentation, p$fbs_6_months, paired = TRUE)
d_pt   <- mean(p$fbs_presentation - p$fbs_6_months) / sd(p$fbs_presentation - p$fbs_6_months)
mw     <- wilcox.test(glucose_level_mg_d_l ~ past_history_of_diabetes, data = p, conf.int = TRUE)
r_mw   <- wilcox_effsize(p, glucose_level_mg_d_l ~ past_history_of_diabetes)$effsize
ws     <- wilcox.test(p$sbp_presentation, p$sbp_6_months, paired = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
med    <- p |> group_by(past_history_of_diabetes) |> summarise(m = median(glucose_level_mg_d_l), q1 = quantile(glucose_level_mg_d_l, .25), q3 = quantile(glucose_level_mg_d_l, .75))
```

## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Session 2: checking shape and spread; Session 3: category outcomes
- Today: the outcome is a **number**, compared with a benchmark, between **two groups**, or **before and after**
- By the end you can:
  - run the t-test that fits the design, and its **rank-based partner**
  - say what each test **actually compares** (means, a location shift, a pseudo-median)
  - report a **difference with its 95% CI** and an **effect size**
  - tell a **precise** non-significant result from an **imprecise** one
:::

# Topic 1 — One group against a benchmark {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## One-sample t: fasting glucose against 100 mg/dL

```{r}
t.test(p$fbs_presentation, mu = 100)
```

## z or t?

::: {.incremental}
- A **z-test** needs the **population** SD to be **known** in advance; in practice it almost never is
- The SD we compute from our sample is an **estimate** → use the **t-test**, whatever the sample size
- "z if n > 30" is an old shortcut from printed tables: with large n the t and z answers agree anyway, so nothing is gained by switching
:::

::: {.key}
Default: `t.test()`. A z-test only if a published population SD is used, and say so.
:::

## Reading the one-sample result

::: {.eq}
"Mean fasting glucose at presentation was `r f(t_fbs$estimate)` mg/dL (95% CI `r f(t_fbs$conf.int[1])` to `r f(t_fbs$conf.int[2])`), `r f(t_fbs$estimate - 100)` mg/dL above the 100 mg/dL threshold for impaired fasting glucose (one-sample t-test, `r fp(t_fbs$p.value)`)."
:::

- The benchmark must come from **outside** the data (a clinical cut-off, a national survey), chosen **before** the analysis
- The CI is narrow because n is large: the **average** adult here is above the threshold, though many individuals are not

# Topic 2 — Two independent groups {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Welch t: age by diabetes history

```{r}
p |> group_by(past_history_of_diabetes) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(age_of_participants), sd = sd(age_of_participants))
t.test(age_of_participants ~ past_history_of_diabetes, data = p)
```

## Reading it

::: {.eq}
"Adults with a past history of diabetes were older: mean `r f(w_age$estimate[2])` vs `r f(w_age$estimate[1])` years (difference `r f(diff(w_age$estimate))` years, 95% CI `r f(-w_age$conf.int[2])` to `r f(-w_age$conf.int[1])`; Welch t-test, `r fp(w_age$p.value)`; Cohen's d = `r f(abs(d_age$Cohens_d), 2)`)."
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Welch**: the groups are very unequal in size (`r sum(p$past_history_of_diabetes == "yes")` vs `r sum(p$past_history_of_diabetes == "no")`), exactly where Student's t can mislead
- The sign: R reports **no − yes**; turn it round so the sentence reads naturally, and say which way
- d ≈ `r f(abs(d_age$Cohens_d), 1)`: a **large** difference; diabetes becomes more common with age
:::

## Two non-significant results, two different stories

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Fasting glucose, women vs men** (n = `r nrow(p)`)

`r f(t_sexf$estimate[1])` vs `r f(t_sexf$estimate[2])` mg/dL, difference 95% CI `r f(t_sexf$conf.int[1])` to `r f(t_sexf$conf.int[2])`; `r fp(t_sexf$p.value)`

→ **precise**: any difference is under about `r f(max(abs(t_sexf$conf.int)), 0)` mg/dL
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Same, in the `r nrow(dmp)` adults with diabetes**

`r f(t_dmf$estimate[1])` vs `r f(t_dmf$estimate[2])` mg/dL, difference 95% CI `r f(t_dmf$conf.int[1])` to `r f(t_dmf$conf.int[2])`; `r fp(t_dmf$p.value)`

→ **imprecise**: women could be up to `r f(-t_dmf$conf.int[1], 0)` mg/dL lower, or slightly higher
:::
:::

::: {.warn}
Both are "not significant". Only the **confidence interval** tells you whether the study **showed** little difference or simply **could not tell**.
:::

## Mann–Whitney U: glucose by diabetes history

```{r}
p |> group_by(past_history_of_diabetes) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median = median(glucose_level_mg_d_l),
            q1 = quantile(glucose_level_mg_d_l, .25), q3 = quantile(glucose_level_mg_d_l, .75))
wilcox.test(glucose_level_mg_d_l ~ past_history_of_diabetes, data = p, conf.int = TRUE)
```

## What Mann–Whitney actually tests

::: {.incremental}
- It ranks all values and asks whether one group tends to have **higher values** than the other
- It is **not** a test of medians unless the two distributions have the **same shape**
- `conf.int = TRUE` gives the **Hodges–Lehmann** shift: the typical difference between a person in one group and a person in the other
- Effect size **r** = Z / √N: `r f(r_mw, 2)` here (rough guide: 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large)
:::

::: {.eq}
"Glucose was higher in adults with a history of diabetes: median `r med$m[2]` (IQR `r f(med$q1[2], 0)`–`r f(med$q3[2], 0)`) vs `r med$m[1]` (`r med$q1[1]`–`r med$q3[1]`) mg/dL; Mann–Whitney U test, `r fp(mw$p.value)`; Hodges–Lehmann shift `r f(-mw$estimate, 0)` mg/dL (95% CI `r f(-mw$conf.int[2], 0)` to `r f(-mw$conf.int[1], 0)`)."
:::

# Topic 3 — Paired measurements {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Paired t: fasting glucose at presentation and 6 months

```{r}
d <- p$fbs_presentation - p$fbs_6_months
c(mean = mean(d), sd = sd(d), skewness = skew(d))
t.test(p$fbs_presentation, p$fbs_6_months, paired = TRUE)
```

## Reading the paired result

::: {.eq}
"Fasting glucose fell by a mean of `r f(pt$estimate)` mg/dL from presentation to 6 months (95% CI `r f(pt$conf.int[1])` to `r f(pt$conf.int[2])`; paired t-test, `r fp(pt$p.value)`; d~z~ = `r f(d_pt, 2)`)."
:::

::: {.incremental}
- The assumption is about the **differences** (skewness `r f(skew(d), 2)`: fine), not about either column
- The effect size for paired data is **d~z~** = mean difference / SD of the differences
- **Why paired?** Each person is their own control. The visits are strongly correlated (r = `r f(cor(p$fbs_presentation, p$fbs_6_months), 2)`): a person high at presentation stays high
- Ignoring the pairing (Welch) gives a 95% CI of `r f(pt_un$conf.int[1])` to `r f(pt_un$conf.int[2])`, about `r f(diff(pt_un$conf.int) / diff(pt$conf.int), 0)` times **wider**: the between-person spread swamps the change
:::

## Wilcoxon signed-rank: systolic pressure, presentation and 6 months

```{r}
wilcox.test(p$sbp_presentation, p$sbp_6_months, paired = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

- For paired data that are **skewed or have outliers** (SBP at presentation: skewness `r f(skew(p$sbp_presentation), 2)`, up to `r max(p$sbp_presentation)` mmHg)
- Assumes the differences are **roughly symmetric** (skewness `r f(skew(p$sbp_presentation - p$sbp_6_months), 2)`); it estimates the **pseudo-median** fall: `r f(ws$estimate, 0)` mmHg (95% CI `r f(ws$conf.int[1], 0)` to `r f(ws$conf.int[2], 0)`)
- Here the paired t-test would also be fine; with real outliers or a small sample, Wilcoxon is the safer choice

## Which test for two groups?

| Design | Roughly normal | Skewed / outliers / ordinal | Report |
|---|---|---|---|
| One group vs benchmark | one-sample t | one-sample Wilcoxon | mean (95% CI) |
| Two independent groups | **Welch t** | **Mann–Whitney U** | difference in means (95% CI), d; or medians (IQR), HL shift, r |
| Two paired measurements | **paired t** (differences normal) | **Wilcoxon signed-rank** | mean difference (95% CI), d~z~; or pseudo-median |

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("t4q1", "You compare a sample mean with a reference value and estimate the SD from your own 200 participants. Which test?",
         c("A one-sample z-test, because n is more than 30",
           "A one-sample t-test, because the SD is estimated",
           "A paired t-test, because there are two values involved",
           "A Mann-Whitney test, because there is only one group"), answer = 2,
         explain = "The z-test needs a known population SD. An SD estimated from the sample calls for the t-test; with large n the two give nearly the same answer, so there is no reason to switch.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("t4q2", "Study A: p = 0.61, 95% CI for the difference -0.6 to 1.0. Study B: p = 0.13, 95% CI -1.6 to 12.2. Which reading is right?",
         c("Both studies have shown that there is no difference at all",
           "Study B is the stronger evidence because its p is smaller",
           "A shows any difference is small; B cannot rule out a large one",
           "Neither study can be interpreted, since both p-values exceed 0.05"), answer = 3,
         explain = "Non-significant results differ in precision. A's narrow interval rules out a meaningful difference; B's wide interval is compatible with no difference and with a large one.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("t4q3", "Glucose is strongly skewed in both groups and the shapes differ. What does a significant Mann-Whitney test allow you to say?",
         c("The two groups have different median glucose values",
           "One group tends to have higher glucose values than the other",
           "The mean glucose values of the two groups differ significantly",
           "The variances of glucose in the two groups are not the same"), answer = 2,
         explain = "Mann-Whitney compares the ranks: whether values in one group tend to exceed those in the other. It is a test of medians only when the two distributions have the same shape.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_fill("t4q4", "For a paired t-test, the effect size dz is the mean of the differences divided by the standard deviation of the ____ . (one word)",
          accept = c("differences", "difference", "paired differences"),
          explain = "dz = mean difference / SD of the differences. Using the SD of either visit instead gives a different number and must be labelled as such.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("t4q5", "The same adults had systolic pressure measured at presentation and at 6 months; the differences are skewed. Which test fits?",
         c("Mann-Whitney U test on the two sets of measurements",
           "Welch t-test, because the two visits have unequal spread",
           "Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the paired measurements",
           "Chi-square test after splitting each reading at 140"), answer = 3,
         explain = "Same people twice means paired data; with skewed differences, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Mann-Whitney and Welch treat the visits as independent groups, and cutting a number into categories throws information away.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- **t, not z**, whenever the SD comes from your sample
- Two groups: **Welch t** or **Mann–Whitney**; paired: **paired t** (differences normal) or **Wilcoxon signed-rank**
- Every result: the **difference with its 95% CI**, an **effect size**, then p
- A non-significant p with a **wide** CI means "we cannot tell", not "no difference"
:::
